hints: Look closely at what the $(CH_3)_3CO^-$ ion is actually doing to that H atom in the curly arrow diagram.
Notice the lone pair on oxygen forms a new O-H bond as it removes $H^+$, while the C-I bond electrons go fully to $I^-$.
Recall the definition of a Bronsted-Lowry base and check whether this step involves electron-pair sharing, oxidation, or water splitting.
walkthrough:
**Spot the type of reaction**

Look at the starting material and products. We lose H and I from adjacent carbons and gain a C=C double bond.

This is an elimination reaction, specifically dehydrohalogenation to make hex-2-ene:
$$\text{R-CH}_2\text{-CH(I)-CH}_3 \rightarrow \text{R-CH=CH-CH}_3 + \text{H}^+ + \text{I}^-$$

**Follow the curly arrows**

The lone pair on $(CH_3)_3CO^-$ attacks H, taking $H^+$ to form $(CH_3)_3COH$. At the same time the C-H electrons form the C=C bond and the C-I electrons move fully onto iodine to give $:I^-$.

All bond breaking is heterolytic, one atom keeps both electrons, no radicals are formed.

**Apply the Bronsted-Lowry definition**

A Bronsted-Lowry base is a proton ($H^+$) acceptor.

Here:
$$\text{(CH}_3\text{)}_3\text{CO}^- + \text{H}^+ \rightarrow \text{(CH}_3\text{)}_3\text{COH}$$
So $(CH_3)_3CO^-$ is clearly acting as a base, not as an oxidising agent, and water is not involved so it is not hydrolysis.

options.A: Correct. The tert-butoxide ion uses its lone pair to accept $H^+$ from carbon, forming $(CH_3)_3COH$. Accepting a proton is exactly the Bronsted-Lowry definition of a base.
options.B: Incorrect. An oxidising agent gains electrons and causes oxidation number increase in another species. Here there is no electron gain by $(CH_3)_3CO^-$, it simply accepts $H^+$. This is acid-base behaviour, not redox.
options.C: Incorrect. The arrow shows both electrons from the C-I bond moving onto iodine to form $:I^-$. That is heterolytic fission. Homolytic fission would give one electron to each atom and form radicals, which does not happen here.
options.D: Incorrect. Hydrolysis means splitting a bond using water (or aqueous $OH^-$) to introduce an OH group. Here no water is used, no C-OH product is formed from the haloalkane, and an alkene is made by elimination.
